## Overview

`deseq2reports` runs a complete RNA-seq differential expression analysis
starting from a `DESeq2::DESeqDataSet` object: quality control, sample
distance/PCA, differential expression across every pairwise and one-vs-rest
group comparison, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) against MSigDB,
optional WGCNA co-expression module detection, and a self-contained HTML
report -- all through one function call, or through the standalone stage
functions if you want to run/inspect a single step.

## One-command usage

```{r}
library(deseq2reports)
library(DESeq2)

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = counts, colData = coldata, design = ~condition)

out <- run_deseq2_pipeline(
  dds = dds,
  var = "condition",
  design = ~condition,
  filter_method = "cpm",
  cpm_percentile = 0.05,
  batch = "batch",
  batch_method = "limma",
  export_counts = TRUE,
  shrinkage = "ashr",
  ranking = "pxfc",
  collections = c("HALLMARK", "KEGG_MEDICUS"),
  run_wgcna = TRUE,
  save_dir = "results"
)
```

Organism (human/mouse) is auto-detected from `rownames(dds)` via
[detect_organism()] -- there is no `org` argument to set. Detection expects
standard HGNC/MGI gene *symbols* as row names (not Ensembl/Entrez IDs, and
not a mix of organisms); if it can't confidently tell which convention your
gene names follow, it errors rather than guessing.

This writes, under `results/`, one folder per module:

* `qc/` -- `qc_filter_summary.csv`, `qc_steps_summary.csv`, library-size /
  count-distribution PDFs, and `qc.html`
* `distance/` -- PCA / sample-similarity plots and CSVs (shown on the QC page)
* `counts/` -- `counts_raw.csv`, `counts_vst.csv`, `counts_rlog.csv`,
  `counts_cpm.csv` (+ `counts_combat_seq.csv` if `batch` is set) -- see
  [Count table exports](#count-table-exports)
* `diffexp/<comparison>/` -- DE tables and MA/volcano PDFs, plus
  `diffexp.html`
* `pathway/<comparison>/gsea/` -- per-collection GSEA CSVs / barplot PDFs,
  plus `pathway_enrichment.html` -- see
  [Pathway enrichment: MSigDB collections](#pathway-enrichment-msigdb-collections)
* `wgcna/` -- module artifacts and `wgcna.html` when `run_wgcna = TRUE`; see
  [Co-expression modules: WGCNA](#co-expression-modules-wgcna)
* `tf_activity/` -- CollecTRI / ULM artifacts and `tf_activity.html` when
  `run_decoupler = TRUE`
* `index.html` at the root -- run summary with relative links into each
  module folder (see [The multi-page HTML report](#the-multi-page-html-report))
* `logs/run_<timestamp>.log` and `.json` -- a reproducibility record of the
  call, console output, and session info

## Standalone modules

Each stage can also be run independently:

```{r}
dds_qc <- run_qc(dds, var = "condition", filter_method = "cpm", cpm_percentile = 0.05)

counts_out <- run_counts_export(dds_qc, batch = "batch", var = "condition")

dist_out <- run_distance_pca(dds_qc, var = "condition", batch = "batch")

de_out <- run_diffexp_pipeline(dds_qc, var = "condition",
                                comparisons = c("Treated_vs_Control"))

gsea_out <- run_gsea_pipeline(de_out$results, collections = "HALLMARK")

wgcna_out <- run_wgcna_pipeline(dds_qc, var = "condition")

render_report(dds_qc, var = "condition", distance_out = dist_out,
              diffexp_out = de_out, gsea_out = gsea_out, wgcna_out = wgcna_out,
              save_dir = "results")
```

## Gene filtering: `filter_method = NULL` / `"cpm"` / `"count"`

By default, `run_qc()` applies **no low-expression filtering**
(`filter_method = NULL`) -- only the optional mitochondrial/X/Y removal
steps run, if requested. Two filtering strategies are available if you want
to remove lowly-expressed genes, selected via `filter_method`:

* **`"cpm"`**: rank genes by mean counts-per-million (CPM) across all
  samples and remove the bottom `cpm_percentile` fraction (default `0.05`,
  i.e. the lowest-expressed 5% of genes). This adapts automatically to
  sequencing depth without requiring an absolute count threshold to be
  chosen up front.
* **`"count"`**: keep a gene if, in at least one level of `var`, at least
  `min_samples_per_group` samples of that group (default: the size of your
  smallest group) have a raw count `>= min_count` (default `10`). This is a
  per-group, `edgeR::filterByExpr()`-style absolute threshold.

Either way, `run_qc()` writes `qc_count_distribution.pdf`: a density plot of
the per-gene statistic actually used for filtering (log2 mean CPM, or log2
total count), coloured by whether each gene was retained, with a dashed
line marking the cutoff (the `cpm_percentile` cutoff on the CPM path, or
`min_count` as a reference point on the count path), so you can check the
chosen threshold against the real shape of your data rather than trusting a
default blindly. This plot -- and the removal table below -- are always
generated (even when `filter_method = NULL`) and shown in the HTML report
**before** any low-expression removal is applied, so you can see the
pre-filtering distribution and decide whether filtering is warranted.

`run_qc()` also tracks, at every filtering step (mitochondrial removal, X/Y
removal, low-expression removal), how many genes went in, how many were
removed, and the percent removed -- written to `qc_steps_summary.csv` and
attached to the returned `dds` object
(`S4Vectors::metadata(dds)$deseq2reports_qc`). When `render_report()` finds
this metadata (i.e. `dds` was filtered via `run_qc()`), it adds a **Quality
control** section to the HTML report showing this step-by-step removal
table, the current low-expression threshold and how to adjust it, the
count-distribution plot (with cutoff line) positioned before the
low-expression-removal step, and the library-size plot.

Optionally (`add_correlation_heatmap = TRUE`; default `FALSE`), `run_qc()`
also computes a Pearson sample-correlation heatmap on the VST-transformed
(or, with `correlation_transform = "rlog"`, rlog-transformed) expression
matrix, with samples hierarchically clustered by `1 - correlation` distance
and annotated by `var`. This is a quick offline diagnostic for outlier or
mislabelled samples before moving on to PCA, and is written to
`qc_sample_correlation_heatmap.pdf`/`qc_sample_correlation_matrix.csv`
(it is not embedded in the HTML report itself -- the report's own "Sample
QC" section shows the Spearman-based sample similarity heatmap from
`run_distance_pca()`/`plot_sample_similarity()` instead). It can also be
run standalone via `plot_sample_correlation()`.

## Count table exports

`run_counts_export()` (folded into the pipeline via `export_counts = TRUE`,
the default) writes four count tables that are independent of the DESeq2
model itself, for downstream/exploratory use: raw counts, VST-transformed
counts, rlog-transformed counts, and counts-per-million (CPM). If `batch` is
supplied, a fifth table, `counts_combat_seq.csv`, is also written --
batch-corrected raw counts from `sva::ComBat_seq()`, using `var` to protect
the biological groups of interest from the correction. **This table is for
visualization/exploratory tools that expect batch-adjusted integer counts;
it is not used by, and should not be fed into, the actual differential
expression model** -- for the real DE test, put your batch variable directly
in the `design` formula instead (see below).

## Batch correction: visualization vs. the DE model

`batch`/`batch_method` (passed to `run_distance_pca()`, or to the pipeline
directly) apply `limma::removeBatchEffect()` or `sva::ComBat()` to the
VST/rlog matrix used **only** for the PCA plot and sample-similarity heatmap.
This is a visualization aid, not a correction applied to the actual
differential-expression model -- DESeq2's negative-binomial fit needs the
real count noise structure, so a genuine, recorded technical batch variable
should instead be included as a term in the `design` formula (e.g.
`~ batch + condition`) for the real test. Use `batch`/`batch_method` (and
the `combat_seq` count export) only when you have such a variable and it
isn't fully confounded with your biological groups; otherwise, skip it.
When batch correction is applied, `run_distance_pca()` returns (and the
HTML report shows) **both** the batch-corrected PCA plot, scree plot, and
top-loadings plot, and their pre-correction counterparts
(`pca_plot_uncorrected`, `scree_plot_uncorrected`,
`top_loadings_plot_uncorrected`), so the effect of the correction can be
inspected directly rather than taken on faith. The PCA plots are also
returned as interactive `plotly` widgets (`pca_plot_interactive`,
`pca_plot_uncorrected_interactive`) that show the sample name on hover.

## PCA diagnostics: scree plot and top loadings

Beyond the PCA scatterplot and sample-similarity heatmap,
`run_distance_pca()` also returns (and the report shows) a **scree plot**
(percent variance explained per PC, `n_scree_pcs` controls how many PCs are
shown) and a **top-loadings plot** (the genes contributing most to each of
the leading `n_loading_pcs` principal components, `n_top_genes` per PC).
These help decide how many PCs are worth interpreting and which genes are
driving the separation seen in the PCA scatterplot -- both are computed
from base R's `prcomp()` on the VST matrix, with per-PC loadings and
top-gene tables also written to `pca_loadings.csv` and
`pca_top_genes_per_pc.csv`. When batch correction is applied, both are also
computed on the pre-correction matrix (`pca_loadings_uncorrected.csv`,
`pca_top_genes_per_pc_uncorrected.csv`) for comparison.

## Interactive plots and tables in the HTML report

The MA and volcano plots (`plot_ma()`, `plot_volcano()`) carry a hidden
`text` aesthetic (gene name, log2 fold-change, adjusted p-value) that
[make_interactive()] converts into a hoverable `plotly` widget -- the HTML
report shows the interactive version of both plots for every comparison,
so pointing at a dot reveals which gene it is. Both plots colour points by
direction (red = up, blue = down, grey = not significant, using the `sig`
column already computed by [run_diffexp()]) and annotate the number of
up- and down-regulated genes directly on the plot. `plot_ma()` uses log2
mean CPM (across all samples in the original, unfiltered dataset) on the
x-axis rather than DESeq2's own `baseMean` -- CPM is comparable across
comparisons, whereas `baseMean` is re-estimated per comparison under
one-vs-rest contrasts and so isn't. The volcano plot itself is styled
after the conventions popularised by the `EnhancedVolcano` package: grey/
red/blue points by direction at a fixed alpha with a thin dark outline,
dashed significance/LFC threshold lines, and a symmetric x-axis
(`max(abs(xmin), abs(xmax))` on both sides).

Rather than a static top-N table, the report's per-comparison DEG table is
a full, unfiltered, sortable/searchable `DT::datatable()`
(`make_deg_datatable()`), so every tested gene -- not just the top hits --
can be found by column sort or text search.

GSEA barplots (`plot_gsea_barplot()`) always show the top 10 up- and top
10 down-regulated pathways by NES, **regardless of significance**, with
black-outlined bars on a continuous red/blue NES scale that is symmetric
about zero (matching a symmetric NES axis range, so up- and
down-regulated bars carry equal visual weight), pathway names drawn
in-plot rather than as axis labels, and significance stars
(`*`/`**`/`***`) placed just beyond each bar's tip, hjust-ed away from the
bar so they don't get clipped or overlap it. Alongside the barplot, the
top/bottom-N pathway table (`gsea_top_bottom_table()`) is rendered as a
sortable/searchable `DT::datatable()` (`make_gsea_datatable()`), styled
the same way as the DEG table. In the HTML report, PCA is split into two
tabs ("After batch correction" / "Before batch correction", the latter
only meaningfully different when `batch` is set) each bundling the PCA
scatter (with dotted zero-reference lines at PC1 = 0 / PC2 = 0), scree
plot, and top-loadings plot together, the sample-similarity heatmap is
shown on its own (the redundant Pearson `plot_sample_correlation()` tab
from `run_qc()` was dropped from the report, though the function itself
remains available standalone), and both the differential expression and
GSEA sections are split into a "Pairwise" and a "One vs. all" subsection
(per [classify_comparison_type()]'s reading of the `"+"` marker in each
comparison name), with one tab per comparison inside each.

## Pathway enrichment: MSigDB collections

`collections` (passed to `run_gsea_pipeline()`, or to the pipeline
directly) accepts one or more of `"HALLMARK"`, `"GOBP"`, `"GOCC"`,
`"GOMF"`, `"KEGG_MEDICUS"`, `"KEGG_LEGACY"`, `"REACTOME"` -- GSEA runs
independently for every requested collection, against every comparison,
writing a separate `<comparison>/gsea/<collection>_gsea.csv` (and
barplot) for each. `run_deseq2_pipeline()`'s own default is
`c("GOBP", "GOCC", "GOMF", "KEGG_MEDICUS", "KEGG_LEGACY", "REACTOME")`
(`"HALLMARK"` remains available but is not forced on by default). In the
HTML report, the "Pathway Enrichment" section nests a tab per collection
inside each comparison's tab, and each barplot's title is just the
comparison name (no collection suffix -- the tab itself already
identifies the collection). Organism (human/mouse, needed to pick the
right `msigdbr` species) is auto-detected from the gene symbols in the
differential-expression results, not passed explicitly -- see
[detect_organism()].

## Co-expression modules: WGCNA

Setting `run_wgcna = TRUE` on the pipeline (or calling
`run_wgcna_pipeline()` directly on a QC'd `dds`) adds a weighted gene
co-expression network analysis:

```{r}
wgcna_out <- run_wgcna_pipeline(
  dds_qc,
  var = "condition",
  power = NULL, # NULL auto-selects via the scale-free-topology criterion
  min_module_size = 30,
  save_dir = "results/wgcna"
)
```

This picks a soft-thresholding power (`pick_wgcna_power()`, plotted by
`plot_soft_threshold()`), detects co-expression modules
(`WGCNA::blockwiseModules()`), correlates each module's eigengene against
the levels of `var` (`plot_module_trait_heatmap()`), identifies hub genes
per module by eigengene-based connectivity (kME), and runs
over-representation analysis on each real module's gene set against every
requested `ora_collection` (default `c("GOBP", "GOCC", "GOMF",
"KEGG_MEDICUS", "KEGG_LEGACY", "REACTOME")`), plotted as a dot plot
(`plot_module_ora_dotplot()`, x = gene-set size, colour = -log10(padj)).

Modules are renamed from WGCNA's arbitrary colour labels to `"Module 1"`,
`"Module 2"`, ... in descending order of gene count, so `"Module 1"` is
always the largest module regardless of which colour WGCNA happened to
assign it -- the underlying colour is still kept alongside (`module_color`
column of `module_df`) for anyone who wants to cross-reference WGCNA's own
plots. `"grey"`, WGCNA's catch-all label for genes it could not confidently
assign to any real module, is renamed `"Unassigned"` and is **excluded**
from over-representation analysis (it isn't a real co-expression module,
so an enrichment test against it isn't meaningful) -- it still appears in
`module_df`, the module-size bar chart, and the module-trait/eigengene
heatmaps. The returned list's `module_df`, `MEs`, `module_trait_cor`, and
`hub_genes` are all consistently keyed by this `"Module N"`/`"Unassigned"`
naming; `ora_by_module` and `ora_plots_by_module` are keyed first by
collection and then by module (`ora_by_module[[collection]][[module]]`),
with `"Unassigned"` absent from both. In the HTML report, this becomes a
"Co-expression modules (WGCNA)" section (shown only when `wgcna_out` is
supplied to `render_report()`, on its own `wgcna.html` page -- see [The
multi-page HTML report](#the-multi-page-html-report)) with the module-size
bar chart, the condition-level module-trait correlation heatmap, and a
sample-level module-eigengene heatmap (samples clustered hierarchically,
so co-varying samples/modules are visually grouped), followed by two
tabbed subsections:

* **"Module genes"**, a top-level section tabbed by module (one tab per
  entry in `hub_genes`, including `"Unassigned"`), listing each module's
  hub genes. This is pulled out as its own section -- rather than nested
  inside per-collection pathway-enrichment tabs, as it was previously --
  since hub genes are a property of the module itself, independent of
  which MSigDB collection (if any) is being tested against it.
* **"Per-module pathway enrichment"**, tabbed **module first, then
  collection nested within each module's tab**
  (`module -> collection`, e.g. "Module 1" > "Collection: GOBP"),
  matching the comparison-then-collection tab nesting used on the
  pathway-enrichment page for differential-expression GSEA results (see
  [The multi-page HTML report](#the-multi-page-html-report)) -- so both
  pages group by the same top-level axis (module vs. comparison) with
  collection as the nested dimension, rather than the WGCNA page using
  the opposite (collection-first) order. `"Unassigned"` has no tab here,
  since it has no coherent expression profile and pathway enrichment
  against it would not be biologically meaningful.

## The multi-page HTML report

`render_report()` writes each section page into its module folder under
`save_dir`, plus `index.html` at the root: `qc/qc.html` (library QC, PCA,
sample-similarity heatmap), `diffexp/diffexp.html` (per-comparison MA /
volcano / DEG table), `pathway/pathway_enrichment.html` (per-comparison,
per-collection GSEA), and optionally `wgcna/wgcna.html` /
`tf_activity/tf_activity.html`. Every page carries the same navigation bar
at the top (current page shown in bold, the others as relative links;
omitted modules are greyed out rather than removed), and every page is
rendered with `self_contained = TRUE`, so each one opens standalone --
offline, no server -- and the whole folder tree can be copied and still
cross-link correctly. `render_report()` returns a named character vector of
the rendered paths (`"index"`, `"qc"`, `"diffexp"`, `"pathway_enrichment"`,
and, if rendered, `"wgcna"` / `"tf_activity"`).

## Plot geometry: square data panels, axis padding, and the legend-aware plotly canvas

Two related geometry conventions apply across the package's static
(`ggplot2`) figures and the interactive (`plotly`) widgets built from a
subset of them, driven by shared helpers in `R/plot_helpers.R` and
`R/distance.R`.

### Which plots are square, and which are exempt

**Only a narrow, explicitly-scoped set of figures render their data panel
as an exact square** via `ggplot2::theme(aspect.ratio = 1)`
(`square_panel_theme()`): `plot_pca()`, `plot_pca_scree()`,
`plot_pca_top_loadings()`, `plot_ma()`, `plot_volcano()`,
`plot_library_size()`, `plot_count_distribution()`, and the
sample-similarity/sample-correlation `pheatmap`s (squared via matching
`cellwidth`/`cellheight`, since they're always square sample x sample
matrices). Squaring these -- the PCA/QC/DE overview figures users tend to
compare side-by-side, plus the two symmetric sample-by-sample matrices --
keeps their proportions consistent across analyses and comparisons.

**Every WGCNA `ggplot2` figure, and the GSEA barplot, are deliberately
exempt** from square-panel theming: `plot_soft_threshold()`,
`plot_module_sizes()`, `plot_module_trait_heatmap()`,
`plot_module_ora_dotplot()`, and `plot_gsea_barplot()` all carry no
`aspect.ratio` setting and render at `ggplot2`'s natural (data-driven)
aspect ratio instead. The module-eigengene heatmap
(`plot_module_eigengene_heatmap()`, a `pheatmap`) is exempt the same way:
its `cellwidth`/`cellheight` are now sized independently per axis (via
`pheatmap_cell_size()`, applied separately to the sample count and the
module count) rather than solved jointly for a square overall panel --
the helper that previously did that joint solve,
`pheatmap_square_cell_size()`, has been removed. In every one of these
cases the natural, often lopsided aspect ratio (many modules vs. few
samples, or vice versa; a handful of gene sets vs. a long tail) is more
informative than a forced square, and forcing one exaggerated or
compressed the underlying spread.

### Axis padding

**Continuous axes carry zero data-padding by default**
(`scale_x_continuous()`/`scale_y_continuous(expand = zero_expansion())`),
so plotted data touches the panel edge with no blank margin -- this
remains the default for most axes package-wide. **Three axes are the
exception**, using `expansion(mult = c(0.1, 0.1))` (10% headroom on each
side) instead of zero padding: `plot_pca()`'s y-axis, `plot_ma()`'s y-axis
(log2FoldChange), and both axes of `plot_volcano()`. These are exactly the
axes that carry corner- or edge-anchored annotations (the MA/volcano
up/down count labels, and the new direction-arrow annotations described
below) whose neighbouring data points would otherwise be crowded flush
against the panel border; PCA's and MA's *other* axis (x, in both cases)
keeps zero data-padding, since nothing is anchored near it. Wherever an
annotation needs to sit at a fixed position regardless of the data range
(count labels, direction arrows, the module-size/GSEA-barplot count/star
labels), it's anchored at `x = Inf`/`y = -Inf` in npc space
(expansion-independent by construction) rather than relying on axis
expansion alone for clearance. **Discrete/categorical axes are left
alone** for the same reason as before -- e.g. the per-sample x-axis on the
library-size boxplot, or the module/pathway-name axis on the module-size
bar chart and ORA dot plot.

**Boundary-touching markers are not clipped.** Zero data-padding puts the
outermost data value's *coordinate* exactly on the panel border, but a
geom's *rendered extent* (a point marker's radius, an outlined bar's
stroke) can reach beyond that coordinate; `ggplot2`'s default
`coord_cartesian(clip = "on")` would hard-clip it. Every plotting function
whose geoms have rendered extent beyond their data coordinate uses
`unclipped_coord()` (or, after `coord_flip()`, `unclipped_coord_flip()`)
to disable this clipping -- unaffected by the axis-padding changes above,
since it's independent of whether padding is zero or 10%. Two functions
deliberately keep the default `clip = "on"`: `plot_pca_top_loadings()` (a
bare, unstroked `geom_col()`) and `plot_count_distribution()` (a
`colour = NA` `geom_density()` fill with no outline) -- neither has any
rendered extent beyond its data coordinate to protect.

### Up/down direction annotations on MA and volcano plots

`plot_ma()` and `plot_volcano()` each carry, in addition to their existing
corner-anchored "Up: N"/"Down: N" gene-count labels, a pair of
direction-arrow annotations naming which comparison level each direction
corresponds to -- since "up"/"down" only has concrete meaning relative to
which level is the numerator ("test") vs. denominator ("reference") of the
`"<test>_vs_<reference>"` comparison string. On `plot_ma()` these sit on
the **left side** of the panel (distinct from the right-anchored count
labels): an upward arrow reading "Higher in `<test>`" near the top, a
downward arrow reading "Higher in `<reference>`" near the bottom. On
`plot_volcano()` they sit **just under the title, at the top of the
panel**: a rightward arrow naming the test level, a leftward arrow naming
the reference level. Both use the same `x = -Inf`/`y = Inf` (or
`x = Inf`/`y = -Inf`) npc-space anchoring as the count labels, so their
position is independent of the data range and cannot collide with the
`ggrepel`-placed gene-symbol labels regardless of where those cluster.

### The legend-aware plotly canvas (`make_interactive()`)

[make_interactive()] converts a static `ggplot` into a hoverable `plotly`
widget for the MA, volcano, and PCA plots. Getting a *square data panel*
in the interactive version is not as simple as carrying over
`theme(aspect.ratio = 1)`: `plotly::ggplotly()` silently drops it (no
error -- the setting just never reaches the built widget), and the
natural-looking substitute, `scaleanchor`/`scaleratio`, only locks the
x/y axes to a 1:1 *data-unit* ratio (like `coord_equal()`), which
reproduces a square *panel* only by coincidence when the x- and y-data
ranges happen to match -- they generally don't for these plots. A second,
easy-to-miss failure mode is the legend: even a canvas sized to be
square, once a categorical legend (e.g. up/down/not-significant colour)
is added, renders with a non-square *interior* data panel once the
legend's real width is carved out of the canvas -- something plotly's own
layout never budgets for server-side.

`make_interactive()`'s `square = TRUE` (the default) solves both
problems together (`.square_plotly_canvas()`): it renders the plot once
without a legend to read back the resolved axis margins from
`plotly::plotly_build()`, estimates the legend's rendered width from its
title/entry text via font-metrics (`graphics::strwidth()`,
`.estimate_legend_width_px()`), and then solves an explicit canvas
width/height and an expanded right margin such that the *data panel* --
the margin-subtracted paper area, excluding axis-label whitespace and the
legend -- is an exact square, with the legend pinned just outside it at
`legend.x > 1` (paper coordinates, sitting in that right margin). The
returned widget always carries this solved size as an explicit fixed pixel
`width`/`height`, together with `plotly::config(responsive = FALSE)`, so
it does not rescale when the browser window is resized -- every plotly
widget in the HTML report renders at a fixed pixel size regardless of
viewport.

## Download buttons in the report

Every table and static figure in the report is paired with a "Download
CSV" or "Download PDF" button (`download_table_button()`,
`download_plot_button()` for `ggplot` figures, `download_grid_plot_button()`
for non-`ggplot` grid-drawables like the sample-similarity `pheatmap`)
positioned in the top-right corner of its figure/table via
`wrap_with_corner_button()`, built on `downloadthis::download_this()`.
Each button embeds its payload directly (`self_contained = TRUE`) so it
works from each fully-offline HTML page this package produces -- no
server or external file reference is involved, and any one of the 5 pages
can be emailed or archived on its own with every underlying table/figure
on it still individually downloadable.

## Arguments people typically change per analysis

| Argument | Where | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `var`, `design` | all stages | grouping column and DESeq2 model formula |
| `comparisons` | diffexp | restrict to specific contrasts instead of all pairwise + one-vs-rest |
| `filter_method`, `cpm_percentile`, `min_count`, `min_samples_per_group` | `run_qc()` | low-expression filtering strategy: none (default), CPM percentile, or per-group raw count |
| `remove_mt`, `remove_xy` | `run_qc()` | gene exclusion (mitochondrial / sex chromosome) |
| `export_counts` | pipeline / `run_counts_export()` | write raw/VST/rlog/CPM (+ ComBat_seq) count tables |
| `batch`, `batch_method` | `run_distance_pca()` | visualization-only batch correction (`limma`/`combat`/`none`) |
| `shrinkage` | `run_diffexp()`/`run_diffexp_pipeline()` | LFC shrinkage estimator: `ashr` (default, supports pooled contrasts), `apeglm` (pairwise only), `normal`, `none` |
| `alpha`, `lfc_threshold` | diffexp | significance thresholds |
| `ranking` | diffexp/GSEA | DEG/GSEA ranking metric: `pxfc`, `padj`, `log2FoldChange`, `stat` |
| `collections` | GSEA | MSigDB collections: one or more of `"HALLMARK"`, `"GOBP"`, `"GOCC"`, `"GOMF"`, `"KEGG_MEDICUS"`, `"KEGG_LEGACY"`, `"REACTOME"` |
| `run_wgcna`, `wgcna_power`, `wgcna_min_module_size` | pipeline / `run_wgcna_pipeline()` | enable co-expression module detection and tune its parameters |
| `pals`, `shape_var` | PCA | plot aesthetics |

## Comparison generation

`generate_comparisons()` derives every pairwise contrast plus one-vs-rest
("pooled") contrasts from the levels of your grouping variable:

```{r}
generate_comparisons(c("Control", "Low", "High"))
# returns every pairwise contrast plus one-vs-rest contrasts, e.g.
# "High_vs_Control", "Control_vs_Low", "High_vs_Low",
# "Control_vs_High+Low", "High_vs_Control+Low", "Low_vs_Control+High"
```

Pooled comparisons merge factor levels by **exact match**, and the model
matrix is checked for full column rank before fitting
(`assert_full_rank_model_matrix()`) so a comparison that would make the
design matrix singular fails immediately with a clear message rather than
deep inside DESeq2.
